steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Hawk and Griffin, language models built on a new gated linear recurrent layer. It should explain why recurrent models are worth revisiting as an alternative to Transformers and end with a numbered list of our main results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- RNNs in early deep learning / NLP; Transformers now dominate
- Transformers struggle with long sequences and slow inference; RNNs as an alternative
- Our contribution: RG-LRU layer, recurrent block, Hawk and Griffin
- Summary of main results (numbered list)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- RNNs in early deep learning / NLP
  - central role early on; practical success, e.g. Google's first end to end machine translation system
  - now Transformer dominates: interleaves MLPs and multi-head attention (MHA)
  - better performance than RNNs, very efficient on modern hardware
  - Transformer LLMs trained on massive web data: remarkable success
- Problems with Transformers
  - quadratic complexity of global attention -> hard to scale to long sequences
  - KV cache grows linearly with sequence length -> slow inference
  - MQA reduces cache by constant factor, still linear growth
  - recurrent LMs: compress whole sequence into fixed-size hidden state, updated iteratively
  - but new RNNs need comparable performance at scale AND similar hardware efficiency
- Our contribution
  - RG-LRU layer: novel gated linear recurrent layer
  - new recurrent block built around it, replaces MQA
  - Hawk: MLPs interleaved with recurrent blocks
  - Griffin: hybrid, MLPs interleaved with recurrent blocks + local attention
- Results
  - power law scaling of held-out loss vs training FLOPs, up to and beyond 7B params (Fig 1(a)), as seen for Transformers
  - Griffin: slightly lower held-out loss than strong Transformer baselines at all scales
  - overtrained on 300B tokens; Hawk-3B beats reported Mamba-3B on downstream tasks with half the tokens; Griffin-7B / 14B match Llama-2 with roughly 7 times fewer tokens (Sec 3.2)
  - training efficiency comparable to Transformers on TPU-v3; diagonal RNN layers memory bound -> Pallas kernel for RG-LRU minimizing memory transfers (Sec 4)
  - inference: significantly higher throughput than MQA Transformers (Fig 1(b)), lower latency sampling long sequences (Sec 5)
  - Griffin better than Transformers on sequences longer than in training; learns copying / retrieval efficiently from training data (Sec 6); but pre-trained models without fine-tuning worse than Transformers on copying and exact-retrieval

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) were very important in the early days of deep learning and NLP research, and they also had practical success in a lot of applications, for example Google's first end to end machine translation system. But in recent years the Transformer architecture has dominated both deep learning and NLP. The Transformer interleaves multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) and multi-head attention (MHA). In practice Transformers get better performance than RNNs and they are also very efficient at using modern hardware. Large language models based on Transformers and trained on massive datasets collected from the web have had remarkable success.

However, Transformers are hard to scale efficiently to long sequences, because global attention has quadratic complexity. Also, the Key-Value (KV) cache grows linearly with the sequence length, and this makes Transformers slow during inference. Multi-Query Attention (MQA) partly helps with this by reducing the cache size by a constant factor, but the cache still grows linearly in sequence length. Recurrent language models are a compelling alternative, since they compress the whole sequence into a fixed-sized hidden state that is updated iteratively. But if new RNN models are going to replace Transformers, they need to show comparable performance at scale and they also need to have similar hardware efficiency.

- Our contribution
  - RG-LRU layer: new gated linear recurrent layer; recurrent block around it replaces MQA
  - Hawk: MLPs + recurrent blocks
  - Griffin: hybrid, MLPs + mix of recurrent blocks and local attention
- Results
  1. power law scaling, held-out loss vs training FLOPs, up to and beyond 7B params (Figure 1(a)), like Transformers
  2. Griffin slightly lower held-out loss than strong Transformer baselines at all scales
  3. overtrain on 300B tokens; Hawk-3B > reported Mamba-3B with half the tokens; Griffin-7B and Griffin-14B match Llama-2 with roughly 7 times fewer tokens (Section 3.2)
  4. training efficiency comparable to Transformers on TPU-v3; memory bound -> Pallas kernel for RG-LRU minimizing memory transfers (Section 4)
  5. inference: much higher throughput than MQA Transformers (Figure 1(b)), lower latency for long samples (Section 5)
  6. Griffin extrapolates better to longer sequences, learns copying/retrieval from training data (Section 6); pre-trained models without fine-tuning worse on copying and exact-retrieval

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) were very important in the early days of deep learning and NLP research, and they also had practical success in a lot of applications, for example Google's first end to end machine translation system. But in recent years the Transformer architecture has dominated both deep learning and NLP. The Transformer interleaves multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) and multi-head attention (MHA). In practice Transformers get better performance than RNNs and they are also very efficient at using modern hardware. Large language models based on Transformers and trained on massive datasets collected from the web have had remarkable success.

However, Transformers are hard to scale efficiently to long sequences, because global attention has quadratic complexity. Also, the Key-Value (KV) cache grows linearly with the sequence length, and this makes Transformers slow during inference. Multi-Query Attention (MQA) partly helps with this by reducing the cache size by a constant factor, but the cache still grows linearly in sequence length. Recurrent language models are a compelling alternative, since they compress the whole sequence into a fixed-sized hidden state that is updated iteratively. But if new RNN models are going to replace Transformers, they need to show comparable performance at scale and they also need to have similar hardware efficiency.

In this work we propose a new gated linear recurrent layer, the RG-LRU layer, and we design a new recurrent block around it which replaces MQA. We use this recurrent block to build two new models. The first one is Hawk, which interleaves MLPs with recurrent blocks. The second one is Griffin, which is a hybrid model that interleaves MLPs with a mix of recurrent blocks and local attention. Our results are the following:

1. Hawk and Griffin show power law scaling between held-out loss and training FLOPs, up to and beyond 7B parameters (Figure 1(a)). This was also observed before for Transformers.

2. At all model scales, Griffin gets slightly lower held-out loss than strong Transformer baselines.

3. We overtrain Hawk and Griffin on 300B tokens at a range of model scales. On downstream tasks Hawk-3B is better than the reported performance of Mamba-3B, even though it is trained on half as many tokens. Griffin-7B and Griffin-14B match the performance of Llama-2 even though they are trained on roughly 7 times fewer tokens (Section 3.2).

4. Hawk and Griffin both have training efficiency comparable to Transformers on TPU-v3. Diagonal RNN layers are memory bound, so to get this we use a kernel for the RG-LRU layer, implemented in Pallas, which minimizes memory transfers (Section 4).

5. At inference time, Hawk and Griffin both have significantly higher throughput than MQA Transformers (Figure 1(b)), and they also have lower latency when sampling long sequences (Section 5).

6. When it is evaluated on sequences longer than the ones seen in training, Griffin performs better than Transformers, and it can also learn copying and retrieval tasks efficiently from training data (Section 6). However, when we evaluate pre-trained models on copying and exact-retrieval tasks without fine-tuning, Hawk and Griffin do less well than Transformers.

steps.text:

In practice Transformers get better performance than RNNs and they are also very efficient at using modern hardware [9]. Large language models based on Transformers and trained on massive datasets collected from the web have had remarkable success [10,11,12,13,14,15].

However, Transformers are hard to scale efficiently to long sequences, because global attention has quadratic complexity. Also, the Key-Value (KV) cache grows linearly with the sequence length, and this makes Transformers slow during inference. Multi-Query Attention (MQA) [16] partly helps with this by reducing the cache size by a constant factor, but the cache still grows linearly in sequence length. Recurrent language models are a compelling alternative, since they compress the whole sequence into a fixed-sized hidden state that is updated iteratively. But if new RNN models are going to replace Transformers, they need to show comparable performance at scale and they also need to have similar hardware efficiency [17,18,19,20,21,22,23].

In this work we propose a new gated linear recurrent layer, the RG-LRU layer, and we design a new recurrent block around it which replaces MQA. We use this recurrent block to build two new models. The first one is Hawk, which interleaves MLPs with recurrent blocks. The second one is Griffin, which is a hybrid model that interleaves MLPs with a mix of recurrent blocks and local attention [24]. 1. Hawk and Griffin show power law scaling between held-out loss and training FLOPs, up to and beyond 7B parameters (Figure 1(a)). This was also observed before for Transformers [9].

2. At all model scales, Griffin gets slightly lower held-out loss than strong Transformer baselines.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) played a central role in the early days of deep learning and NLP research [1,2,3,4,5,6], and had practical success in many applications, including Google's first end to end machine translation system [7]. However in recent years, both deep learning and NLP have been dominated by the Transformer architecture [8], which interleaves multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) and multi-head attention (MHA). Transformers achieve better performance than RNNs in practice and are also very efficient at using modern hardware [9]. Transformer-based large language models trained on massive datasets collected from the web have achieved remarkable success [10,11,12,13,14,15].

Despite their successes, Transformers are difficult to scale efficiently to long sequences because of the quadratic complexity of global attention. In addition, the linear growth of the Key-Value (KV) cache with the sequence length makes Transformers slow during inference. Multi-Query Attention (MQA) [16] partially mitigates this by reducing the cache size by a constant factor, but the cache still grows linearly in sequence length. Recurrent language models are a compelling alternative, as they compress the entire sequence into a fixed-sized hidden state which is updated iteratively. However, to replace Transformers, new RNN models must show not only comparable performance at scale but also similar hardware efficiency [17,18,19,20,21,22,23].

In this work, we propose the RG-LRU layer, a novel gated linear recurrent layer, and design a new recurrent block around it to replace MQA. We build two new models with this recurrent block: Hawk, a model which interleaves MLPs with recurrent blocks, and Griffin, a hybrid model which interleaves MLPs with a mixture of recurrent blocks and local attention [24]. We show that:

1. Hawk and Griffin exhibit power law scaling between held-out loss and training FLOPs, up to and beyond 7B parameters (Figure 1(a)), as was previously observed for Transformers [9].

2. Griffin achieves slightly lower held-out loss than strong Transformer baselines at all model scales.

3. We overtrain Hawk and Griffin on 300B tokens at a range of model scales. Hawk-3B exceeds the reported performance of Mamba-3B [23] on downstream tasks, despite being trained on half as many tokens. Griffin-7B and Griffin-14B match the performance of Llama-2 [13] while being trained on roughly 7 times fewer tokens (Section 3.2).

4. Hawk and Griffin both achieve training efficiency comparable to Transformers on TPU-v3. Since diagonal RNN layers are memory bound, we achieve this with a kernel for the RG-LRU layer, implemented in Pallas [25], that minimizes memory transfers (Section 4).

5. During inference, Hawk and Griffin both achieve significantly higher throughput than MQA Transformers (Figure 1(b)), and lower latency when sampling long sequences (Section 5).

6. Griffin performs better than Transformers when evaluated on sequences longer than those seen during training, and can also efficiently learn copying and retrieval tasks from training data (Section 6). However, Hawk and Griffin perform less well than Transformers when pre-trained models are evaluated on copying and exact-retrieval tasks without fine-tuning.
